title: Regression Models and Life-Tables
venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Methodological)
harvard_reference: Cox, D.R. (1972) 'Regression models and life-tables', Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Methodological), 34(2), pp. 187-202. doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1972.tb00899.x.
abstract_summary: Cox considers how to analyse censored failure times when each individual has one or more explanatory variables. In his model the hazard function (age-specific failure rate) is a function of the explanatory variables and unknown regression coefficients, multiplied by an arbitrary and unknown function of time: lambda(t; z) = exp(z beta) lambda_0(t) (eq. 9, Section 3), where lambda_0(t) is the hazard under the standard conditions z = 0. The paper leaves lambda_0(t) arbitrary, treating it as a nuisance function, and focuses on the regression parameters. To estimate them it conditions on the set of observed failure times and on the individuals still at risk at each one. This gives a conditional likelihood, later called the partial likelihood, that does not involve lambda_0(t) (Section 5, eqs 12-13), along with score and information expressions and a score test of beta = 0. The paper also extends the Kaplan-Meier product-limit approach and two-sample life-table comparisons, allows time-dependent covariates, and outlines some generalisations. It was read before the Royal Statistical Society on 8 March 1972 and printed with a published discussion.

claims_supported.claim: The proportional-hazards model relates covariates to the hazard of an event multiplicatively without specifying the baseline hazard, and handles censored observations.
claims_supported.where: All three parts are stated explicitly. (a) Multiplicative covariate effect on the hazard. Summary (p. 187): the hazard is 'taken to be a function of the explanatory variables and unknown regression coefficients multiplied by an arbitrary and unknown function of time'. Section 3 'Regression Models' (p. 189), eq. (9): lambda(t; z) = exp(z beta) lambda_0(t). Example 1 on the same page shows the two-sample hazards as lambda_0(t) and psi lambda_0(t) with psi = e^beta, and Example 2 names this 'a simple model of proportional hazards'. (b) Baseline hazard left unspecified. Section 3 (p. 189): lambda_0(t) 'is an unknown function' giving the hazard under z = 0. Section 4 'Analysis of Regression Models' (p. 190) says the paper will 'concentrate on exploring the consequence of allowing lambda_0(t) to be arbitrary', with lambda_0(t) treated as a nuisance function. Section 5 'A Conditional Likelihood' (pp. 190-191, eqs 12-13) builds a likelihood for beta that does not involve lambda_0(t), 'a method of analysis holding for all lambda_0(t)'. (c) Censoring. The Summary opens with 'The analysis of censored failure times is considered'. Section 1 (p. 187) defines censoring: for censored individuals 'we know only that the time to failure is greater than the censoring time'. Section 2 (p. 188) defines the risk set R(t), which includes individuals whose failure or censoring time is at least t, and this risk set enters the conditional likelihood in eqs (12)-(13). One point of wording: the phrase 'proportional-hazards model' is the later standard name. Cox himself calls it a regression model for the hazard and uses 'proportional hazards' only in passing (p. 189). This does not undermine the claim.

caveats: 1) The 1972 paper calls the estimating function a 'conditional likelihood'. The term 'partial likelihood' and its formal justification come from Cox (1975, Biometrika 62(2), pp. 269-276). If the report uses the phrase 'partial likelihood', cite Cox (1975) as well, or keep to 'conditional likelihood' when citing only this paper. 2) Cox allows the covariates z to depend on time (p. 189), so the model is not limited to strictly proportional hazards. The proportional-hazards assumption holds only when the covariates are fixed over time, and the report should say it tested that assumption, for example with Schoenfeld residuals, which are not in this paper. 3) Cox's handling of censoring assumes that a censored individual's only information is that failure had not happened by the censoring time (p. 188). This is commonly read as non-informative censoring, although on p. 191 Cox does not require censoring times to be independent of z. In the Telco data, customers who have not churned are censored at their current tenure, which is administrative right-censoring. 4) The paper's examples are medical and reliability data, not customer churn. Applying the model to churn is the report's own step, and published churn-survival studies should be cited for it. 5) Tied failure times are handled separately in the paper (discrete-time conditioning, mentioned on pp. 190-191). The Telco 'tenure' field is recorded in whole months and has many ties, so the report should name the tie-handling method its software uses (Breslow or Efron). Those methods are not described in the pages checked here.
